Bio Farming

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Science Fiction meets reality, we have done those stories internationally, and been amazed at the world of innovation being used in the medical arena.

But right on our doorstep in Cape Town is a genuinely disruptive technology that is changing the way we make, store and distribute pharmaceuticals.

In 2014 Belinda Shaw went to a TED talk in Cape Town, Prof Ed Rybicki from UCT took the floor, with two questions:
What if there was a way to make complex pharmaceuticals inexpensive?
What if we could do them right here in Cape Town, South Africa; the continent?

Prof Ed Rybicki and his team at BRU (Biopharming Research Unit) had developed a world class way of developing vaccines and anti- bodies in tobacco plants (actually a weedy relative of the tobacco plant Nicotiana Benthamiana). BRU in fact held an incredible patent portfolio for their research which was being sold off shore for commercial production. FOR EXAMPLE: their key patent for developing flu vaccines in plants went overseas. There was very little local interest to develop their research from lab scale to commercial mainly due to the costs involved. Another case of incredible South African inventions, research and innovations that end up being made internationally.

Belinda felt a critical need to retain valuable IP (Intellectual Property) where it belonged – in South Africa. She set about investigating, - the potential of commercialising Ed’s research…looking for funding, for partners, for clients. There was/and is no question that the technology developed by Ed and his team at BRU is disruptive technology in that plant made proteins (used to make vaccines and antibodies) can be made cheaper faster and safer and often better than the traditional way which needs vast funds to set up vast sterile laboratories with enormous steel containers/ fermenters.


Further information:
It wasn’t easy, she was entering a totally new field but finally four years later with the backing of UCT, she raised the funding from the Department of Trade and Industry’s THRIP programme (Technology and Human Resources for Industry Programme). Her partnership with BRU, with commercial interest, had the viability to get her project on the road.


And so the idea became the reality, Cape Bio Pharms was born.

Today they have the only indoor hydro phonic farm on the continent to grow pharmaceuticals and industrial vaccines and antibodies.

The key attraction was having UCT as their research partner and providing employment for their MSc graduates.    Critical was having Profession Ed Rybicki and his team fully behind them- Ed is one of the world’s leading scientists in Molecular Biology - he’s just received the NRF A rating award for research excellence.

By the end of October, early November they will have a greenhouse full of plants at different stages of growth with one batch ready for the infiltration of the proteins which is key to this process – ( This is also the time to film the visuals and the process which in itself is a revolutionary process according to Ed Rybecki) the plants take 6/7 weeks to get fully developed for the infiltration of the proteins.
The essence for Belinda was that UCT’s Bio Farming research unit had developed the largest portfolio of patents for transient expression technology i.e. expressing a wide variety of proteins in plants - this cover the full spectrum of our proteins i.e. various antibodies as well as for animal and human vaccines.  Shockingly though BRU could not get any local companies interested in commercialising this potential.  

The traditional or antiquated way of producing vaccines and antibodies is in living systems, bacteria, yeast, eggs.. this has been preferred way for around 70 years. This process needs huge laboratories, with big containers and very sterile conditions and cost a mint to set up; minimum 100 000 USD.

Bio Farming - Using the plant as a factory, on the other hand needs very little to set up. The heart of this technology is the humble plant cell. The wonderful thing about plants is that they are as complicated as yeast or mammalian cells but they have internal bacteria that act as batteries (Chloroplast). Chloroplasts take light, carbon dioxide and water and they convert it into sugars you just have to provide really simple ingredients and shine a light on the plant and it produces complex chemicals.
Sterile conditions are not a necessity because the plant itself protects the growing proteins.

It is a scalable technique you need 6 to 7 weeks to produce a new batch of proteins a very important factor: Case in point - During the 2010 World Cup soccer event the government ordered a million doses of the H1 N1 flue vaccine. It never arrived….The SARS flue epidemic had just wiped out over 200 000 people in Asia so South Africa was last on the list of vaccines.

South Africa at the time had no vaccine producing capabilities putting us at a distinct disadvantage if ever a pandemic where to hit our shores.  Flu vaccines are traditionally made in fermentation systems that can take up to seven months to product.  Its a hit and miss if they’ve predicted the right strain.  

We will tell the story of the start up of their Bio Farm, their vision and funding challenges interviewing Belinda Shaw ( CEO ) and Tamlyn her daughter who after graduating from UCT with an MSc in Medical Biochemistry left South Africa because of the impossibility of work in this field. She returned when this project became viable and is now the Head Scientist.

Their funding also provides for two Masters Bursaries – and have two students - Siphumelele and Asanda - who are now completing their Masters under their bursary funding.  There is also Bulelani, who is being trained up as the grow room supervisor (Bulelani was a street kid - put himself through school and matriculated.  He still lives at the shelter in town but they are trying to find him more suitable accommodation)

We will visit the BioPharming Reserch Unit at UCT where we will interview Prof Ed Rybicki on his journey, his patents and future of plant based vaccines and antibodies. He could talk about some of his patents that have been licened outside South Africa
(like - he could refer to the licensing of some of their products to Kentucky Bio. (recipients of USA Defence money to produce a million vaccine doses in a month)

We will film the process the grow room set up, plants being seeded, transferred to grow room, and also batch being sent through for infiltration using the transient expression technology – this is a very innovative and part of Prof Ed Rybecki’s patent.

We will not lack for visuals in the telling of this story. With close up visuals of the plants and the process; graphics re what is happening; also we have visuals of the very start of this Bio Pharm, from seedlings to full growth in this futuristic plant farm.

CSIR, like BRU have also been researching this technology. They’ve produced a potential diagnostic protein for rabies - called rabivir. Tsepo Tsekoa is a key scientist and inventor behind this. There is a possibility of this also being produced commercially by Cape Bio Farms and so keeping another valuable patent on SA soil.

South Africa has a new Bio Economy strategy which specifically focuses on biopharming, Dr Ben Durham is the author of this and we could interview him to get the broader SA government strategic point of view.

Press Release:


Bio Pharming
Vaccines and antibodies growing in plants? That’s the revolutionary disruptive development that a hydroponic farm in the Cape is pioneering. The traditional method of producing vaccines and antibodies has always been in living systems – bacteria, yeast and eggs – now tobacco plants have become the conduit for creating life-saving vaccines. It’s a development so remarkable, that it could help wipe out African Horse Sickness, a disease so deadly it’s a scourge for horses in Sub Saharan Africa – and it’s only the beginning.
Producer: Diana Lucas
Presenter: Derek Watts
Watch the trailer



Script:


Bio Pharm

Link: On the face of it, there seems nothing out of the ordinary about this hydroponic farm in the Cape, but these plants- are not being grown for food they are actually vaccine factories in the making.

V/O
It’s called Bio Pharming, turning plants into medicine factories and it’s a technology that will change the face of the pharmaceutical industry.

Link: For around 70 years the method of making vaccines has not changed much they are made in animal cells, yeast, bacteria and even insects, the traditional flu vaccine is made in eggs but you need one egg for each dose of vaccine…

Prof Ed Rybicki: Its an expensive process. You need big capacity and that costs couple of 100 million USD a time and that’s for a reasonably small vaccine factory.

V/O 13 sec
Ed Rybicki heads up the BioPharming Research Unit or BRU at the University of Cape Town, his pioneering work on how to make vaccines in plants goes back to the early 90’s.

Prof Ed Rybicki: I was a plant virologist who slowly got into human and animal virology then the fact that we could use what I already knew how to do to make something that was the field that I had moved into was really appealing

V/O 11 sec
Ed with his team at BRU were one of three international groups leading the field in growing vaccines and antibodies in plants…like the vaccine for the flu virus.

Link
It sounds unbelievable to draw a link between the 2010 World Cup and producing vaccines but behind the football matches there was a major international panic

V/O 10 sec
At a Health Conference at the Waterfront the concern was that South Africa would not be prepared if a flu pandemic hit the country during the world cup

Prof Ed Rybicki: So we had an emergency meeting because there had been this growing outbreak of bird flu and we thought what capacity does SA have to respond to that and it turned out none at all so we thought let’s look at it in plants.

V/O 7 sec
The plant they used is a weedy cousin of the tobacco plant called Nicotiania Benthamiana.
( pronounce as Nikotiana Benthamiaana)

Ed: Its reasonably easily to cultivate The interesting thing is it is an Australian Desert Plant and its thrown away a whole lot of it’s defence mechanisms to survive in the desert so it’s a really good lab rat in terms of being able to make things but in a decent size plant.

V/O 7 sec
The process starts with infiltrating the DNA of the vaccine they want to grow into the leaf of the plant.

Ed : you are putting just about every cell in the plant leaf in contact with bacteria that put DNA into them that allows you to make protein from that moment forward. So in the next 7 odd days that plant is now making the protein that you want.

Link: Within a month Ed’s team at BRU had been able to produce a flu vaccine grown in a plant like this but just as quickly the patent was snapped up and taken off shore.

Prof Ed Rybicki: There was no capacity to do anything further in this country we had a product we proved it did all the right thing in terms of what a flu vaccine should do but so it sat there as a patent until a company came and talked to us quietly and said can we license this.

V/O
In 2014, Environmental Journalist and television producer, Belinda Shaw attended a lecture of Ed’s.

Belinda: There on stage was Prof Ed Rybicki talking about producing vaccines in tobacco plants and the fact that we had no vaccine producing capabilities in this country so we can get caught high and dry when there is a pandemic this blew me away.

V/O 5 sec
And despite Ed’s numerous patents on plant based vaccines, we were not making them.

Link: What really enraged Belinda was South African scientists had spent years developing valuable technology that was being lost overseas but should have be used commercially here at home

Derek: You didn’t want it going overseas?
Belinda: No that irritates me when we have got so many clever people in this country producing such incredible technology but we are losing the IP to somebody overseas that is prepared to run with it.

V/O 17 sec
Her vision: to create a proudly South Africa Bio Pharm. It took three years until finally, with the backing of UCT Belinda raised the funding from the Department of Trade and Industry’s THRIP programme and Cape Bio Pharms became a reality.

Prof Ed Ribicki: So the UCT and Cape Bio Pharms this brand new entity are now together in this venture.

Belinda: We start slow and then we start moving up the ladder. So we start with what is called a re agent or antibody.

Link: When we talk about antibodies it sounds very complicated but they are part of our immune system to fight diseases they can also act as tiny detectives in diagnostic kits as they change colour when they find their targets.

Belinda: Their isn’t a lab in the world when they are looking to produce a new drug that doesn’t need an antibody and then we will move up ladder into diagnostics so when you go and have a strip test to see if you have got diabetes or HIV that protein on that strip is what we can grow in plants.

Tamlyn: We are the first of its kind on the continent and we are hoping this technology can spread through out the world because its so much cheaper to produce through plants compared to the currents systems.

V/O 6 sec
Tamlyn Shaw, Belinda’s daughter is the senior scientist and a big part of Belinda’s mission.

Belinda: You know there are so many masters and students coming out really qualified in the Bio Science and they can’t find a job so Tamlyn is my partner and my daughter and how amazing is this that this could provide jobs for not only her but S and F some of the brightest guys I know and have done their masters in this particular technology

Link

Francisco: What really excites me is application of it plants are very easy to grow and the potential is world wide.

V/O 9 sec
And producing these pharmaceuticals in plants costs way less as much as 1000 times less - a huge factor in scaling up.

Ed: I can start with something the size of this table, I can scale it up to a big green house and it doesn’t have to be sterile and you don’t need vast amounts of stainless steel and you don’t need expensive growth media which you need for any cell based product.

V/O 8 sec
To Infuse large quantities of plants with the DNA of the vaccine or antibody, a vacuum infiltration system is used….

Scott: We put what actually gets into plants… trick the plants
Bacterium double tricks the plant and bacteria
We’ve put the DNA in and all the plant cells does is read the DNA what we told it to make.
Tamlyn: We dunk the plants into the solution of bacteria upside down we apply a negative vacuum pressure and sucks all the air out of the leaves and then we re apply the pressure the bacteria rush into the plant.

Link When you talk about infusing the leaves with protein of the plant it sounds complicated but watch this.

…they flouresce

V/O 11 sec
Consistency is key in growing the plants LED lights are coloured blue for seedlings, red to help the leaves grow and white when they need to stabilise the plant.

Derek: Close to plants?
Belinda: I get quiet upset when we have to harvest them but we do tell them of their journey and at the end of the day they are playing their plant in science.

V/O 9
Getting the protein that makes up the antibodies out of the plants is done in a sterile lab….it starts with making a smoothy from the plant leaves.

Scott: Then its just a matter to extract that protein out of leaves it takes a lot of grinding and processing…

V/O 4 sec
The grant is also funding two students who are doing their Masters at BRU.

Sphu: That’s also quiet inspiring it means what I am doing is actually …going to make a difference as well.

V/O
Last year we investigated the failure of live vaccines in trying to prevent African Horse Sickness … a scourge for horses in Sub –Saharan Africa…Now BRU working with the CSIR and the University of Pretoria have a successfully tested a plant based vaccine which will go a long way in helping wipe out this deadly disease

Francesco: What it is is basically instead of being a live virus we do everything inside the plant resembles a virus but not actually virus the horses immune system will think it is a virus but it wont c….and the hors will become immunised against it

V/O 13 sec
While BRU have many patents for vaccines that are being developed by big pharmaceutical companies off shore like Medicago for the most Bio Pharming is still a novelty in the pharmaceutical industry

Prof Ed Rybicki
It’s not being picked up by Big Pharma to some extent because of inertia, they have got 1000 of millions of dollars invested you are coming along saying we can make it differently//
Any disruptive technology has a resistance built in by the status quo. Big Pharma is starting to dip its toe into the water .

Link: What really enraged Belinda was South African scientists had spent years developing valuable technology that was being lost overseas but should have be used commercially here at home Derek: You didn’t want it going overseas? Belinda: No that irritates me when we have got so many clever people in this country producing such incredible technology but we are losing the IP to somebody overseas that is prepared to run with it. V/O 17 sec Her vision: to create a proudly South Africa Bio Pharm. It took three years until finally, with the backing of UCT Belinda raised the funding from the Department of Trade and Industry’s THRIP programme and Cape Bio Pharms became a reality. Prof Ed Ribicki: So the UCT and Cape Bio Pharms this brand new entity are now together in this venture. Belinda: We start slow and then we start moving up the ladder. So we start with what is called a re agent or antibody. Link: When we talk about antibodies it sounds very complicated but they are part of our immune system to fight diseases they can also act as tiny detectives in diagnostic kits as they change colour when they find their targets. Belinda: Their isn’t a lab in the world when they are looking to produce a new drug that doesn’t need an antibody and then we will move up ladder into diagnostics so when you go and have a strip test to see if you have got diabetes or HIV that protein on that strip is what we can grow in plants. Tamlyn: We are the first of its kind on the continent and we are hoping this technology can spread through out the world because its so much cheaper to produce through plants compared to the currents systems. V/O 6 sec Tamlyn Shaw, Belinda’s daughter is the senior scientist and a big part of Belinda’s mission. Belinda: You know there are so many masters and students coming out really qualified in the Bio Science and they can’t find a job so Tamlyn is my partner and my daughter and how amazing is this that this could provide jobs for not only her but S and F some of the brightest guys I know and have done their masters in this particular technology Link Francisco: What really excites me is application of it plants are very easy to grow and the potential is world wide. V/O 9 sec And producing these pharmaceuticals in plants costs way less as much as 1000 times less - a huge factor in scaling up. Ed: I can start with something the size of this table, I can scale it up to a big green house and it doesn’t have to be sterile and you don’t need vast amounts of stainless steel and you don’t need expensive growth media which you need for any cell based product. V/O 8 sec To Infuse large quantities of plants with the DNA of the vaccine or antibody, a vacuum infiltration system is used…. Scott: We put what actually gets into plants… trick the plants Bacterium double tricks the plant and bacteria We’ve put the DNA in and all the plant cells does is read the DNA what we told it to make. Tamlyn: We dunk the plants into the solution of bacteria upside down we apply a negative vacuum pressure and sucks all the air out of the leaves and then we re apply the pressure the bacteria rush into the plant. Link When you talk about infusing the leaves with protein of the plant it sounds complicated but watch this. …they flouresce V/O 11 sec Consistency is key in growing the plants LED lights are coloured blue for seedlings, red to help the leaves grow and white when they need to stabilise the plant. Derek: Close to plants? Belinda: I get quiet upset when we have to harvest them but we do tell them of their journey and at the end of the day they are playing their plant in science. V/O 9 Getting the protein that makes up the antibodies out of the plants is done in a sterile lab….it starts with making a smoothy from the plant leaves. Scott: Then its just a matter to extract that protein out of leaves it takes a lot of grinding and processing… V/O 4 sec The grant is also funding two students who are doing their Masters at BRU. Sphu: That’s also quiet inspiring it means what I am doing is actually …going to make a difference as well. V/O Last year we investigated the failure of live vaccines in trying to prevent African Horse Sickness … a scourge for horses in Sub –Saharan Africa…Now BRU working with the CSIR and the University of Pretoria have a successfully tested a plant based vaccine which will go a long way in helping wipe out this deadly disease Francesco: What it is is basically instead of being a live virus we do everything inside the plant resembles a virus but not actually virus the horses immune system will think it is a virus but it wont c….and the hors will become immunised against it V/O 13 sec While BRU have many patents for vaccines that are being developed by big pharmaceutical companies off shore like Medicago for the most Bio Pharming is still a novelty in the pharmaceutical industry Prof Ed Rybicki It’s not being picked up by Big Pharma to some extent because of inertia, they have got 1000 of millions of dollars invested you are coming along saying we can make it differently// Any disruptive technology has a resistance built in by the status quo. Big Pharma is starting to dip its toe into the water .

metadata.Summary: Science Fiction meets reality, we have done those stories internationally, and been amazed at the world of innovation being used in the medical arena. But right on our doorstep in Cape Town is a genuinely disruptive technology that is changing the way we make, store and distribute pharmaceuticals. In 2014 Belinda Shaw went to a TED talk in Cape Town, Prof Ed Rybicki from UCT took the floor, with two questions: What if there was a way to make complex pharmaceuticals inexpensive? What if we could do them right here in Cape Town, South Africa; the continent? Prof Ed Rybicki and his team at BRU (Biopharming Research Unit) had developed a world class way of developing vaccines and anti- bodies in tobacco plants (actually a weedy relative of the tobacco plant Nicotiana Benthamiana). BRU in fact held an incredible patent portfolio for their research which was being sold off shore for commercial production. FOR EXAMPLE: their key patent for developing flu vaccines in plants went overseas. There was very little local interest to develop their research from lab scale to commercial mainly due to the costs involved. Another case of incredible South African inventions, research and innovations that end up being made internationally. Belinda felt a critical need to retain valuable IP (Intellectual Property) where it belonged – in South Africa. She set about investigating, - the potential of commercialising Ed’s research…looking for funding, for partners, for clients. There was/and is no question that the technology developed by Ed and his team at BRU is disruptive technology in that plant made proteins (used to make vaccines and antibodies) can be made cheaper faster and safer and often better than the traditional way which needs vast funds to set up vast sterile laboratories with enormous steel containers/ fermenters.
metadata.Further information: It wasn’t easy, she was entering a totally new field but finally four years later with the backing of UCT, she raised the funding from the Department of Trade and Industry’s THRIP programme (Technology and Human Resources for Industry Programme). Her partnership with BRU, with commercial interest, had the viability to get her project on the road. And so the idea became the reality, Cape Bio Pharms was born. Today they have the only indoor hydro phonic farm on the continent to grow pharmaceuticals and industrial vaccines and antibodies. The key attraction was having UCT as their research partner and providing employment for their MSc graduates. Critical was having Profession Ed Rybicki and his team fully behind them- Ed is one of the world’s leading scientists in Molecular Biology - he’s just received the NRF A rating award for research excellence. By the end of October, early November they will have a greenhouse full of plants at different stages of growth with one batch ready for the infiltration of the proteins which is key to this process – ( This is also the time to film the visuals and the process which in itself is a revolutionary process according to Ed Rybecki) the plants take 6/7 weeks to get fully developed for the infiltration of the proteins. The essence for Belinda was that UCT’s Bio Farming research unit had developed the largest portfolio of patents for transient expression technology i.e. expressing a wide variety of proteins in plants - this cover the full spectrum of our proteins i.e. various antibodies as well as for animal and human vaccines. Shockingly though BRU could not get any local companies interested in commercialising this potential. The traditional or antiquated way of producing vaccines and antibodies is in living systems, bacteria, yeast, eggs.. this has been preferred way for around 70 years. This process needs huge laboratories, with big containers and very sterile conditions and cost a mint to set up; minimum 100 000 USD. Bio Farming - Using the plant as a factory, on the other hand needs very little to set up. The heart of this technology is the humble plant cell. The wonderful thing about plants is that they are as complicated as yeast or mammalian cells but they have internal bacteria that act as batteries (Chloroplast). Chloroplasts take light, carbon dioxide and water and they convert it into sugars you just have to provide really simple ingredients and shine a light on the plant and it produces complex chemicals. Sterile conditions are not a necessity because the plant itself protects the growing proteins. It is a scalable technique you need 6 to 7 weeks to produce a new batch of proteins a very important factor: Case in point - During the 2010 World Cup soccer event the government ordered a million doses of the H1 N1 flue vaccine. It never arrived….The SARS flue epidemic had just wiped out over 200 000 people in Asia so South Africa was last on the list of vaccines. South Africa at the time had no vaccine producing capabilities putting us at a distinct disadvantage if ever a pandemic where to hit our shores. Flu vaccines are traditionally made in fermentation systems that can take up to seven months to product. Its a hit and miss if they’ve predicted the right strain. We will tell the story of the start up of their Bio Farm, their vision and funding challenges interviewing Belinda Shaw ( CEO ) and Tamlyn her daughter who after graduating from UCT with an MSc in Medical Biochemistry left South Africa because of the impossibility of work in this field. She returned when this project became viable and is now the Head Scientist. Their funding also provides for two Masters Bursaries – and have two students - Siphumelele and Asanda - who are now completing their Masters under their bursary funding. There is also Bulelani, who is being trained up as the grow room supervisor (Bulelani was a street kid - put himself through school and matriculated. He still lives at the shelter in town but they are trying to find him more suitable accommodation) We will visit the BioPharming Reserch Unit at UCT where we will interview Prof Ed Rybicki on his journey, his patents and future of plant based vaccines and antibodies. He could talk about some of his patents that have been licened outside South Africa (like - he could refer to the licensing of some of their products to Kentucky Bio. (recipients of USA Defence money to produce a million vaccine doses in a month) We will film the process the grow room set up, plants being seeded, transferred to grow room, and also batch being sent through for infiltration using the transient expression technology – this is a very innovative and part of Prof Ed Rybecki’s patent. We will not lack for visuals in the telling of this story. With close up visuals of the plants and the process; graphics re what is happening; also we have visuals of the very start of this Bio Pharm, from seedlings to full growth in this futuristic plant farm. CSIR, like BRU have also been researching this technology. They’ve produced a potential diagnostic protein for rabies - called rabivir. Tsepo Tsekoa is a key scientist and inventor behind this. There is a possibility of this also being produced commercially by Cape Bio Farms and so keeping another valuable patent on SA soil. South Africa has a new Bio Economy strategy which specifically focuses on biopharming, Dr Ben Durham is the author of this and we could interview him to get the broader SA government strategic point of view.
